articles.title: Audience imaginaries and convergence culture at the museum
articles.authors: Ea Christina Valentin Willumsen, Nanna Holdgaard
articles.abstract: This article explores how museum audiences imagine the Viking Age and ancient Egypt, and how these imaginaries are shaped and mobilised within a converged media landscape. Drawing on a qualitative study combining creative collage-making, semi-structured interviews, and exhibition walk-alongs with 20 participants, the article analyses the interpretive frameworks that audiences bring into the exhibition. The analysis shows that audience imaginaries are durable and deeply embedded, formed through the interplay of educational experiences, museum encounters, and popular culture over time. New exhibition narratives were most often assimilated into existing imaginaries, contributing incremental adjustments. The article argues that museum exhibitions function as interpretive nodes within a broader media ecology, where meaning is negotiated from within pre-existing imaginative frameworks without being fundamentally redefined.

articles.title: Demythologising through stable diffusion: AI-generated visualisations in Angela Carter’s The Passion of New Eve
articles.authors: Longlong Ge, Lei Yan
articles.abstract: This project draws on Angela Carter’s ‘demythologising business’ to explore how Stable Diffusion (SD), an open-source latent diffusion model, can be critically mobilised for feminist literary criticism. Carter’s demythologisation reveals the constructedness and contingency of patriarchal myths, and unsettles their historical influence on contemporary gendered, ideological, and power structures. In the anti-mythic novel  The Passion of New Eve (1977), Carter reimagines Genesis and Odyssean mythology through Eve(lyn)’s grotesque journey of gender metamorphosis, thereby defamiliarising culturally constructed femininity and rethinking gendered power relations. Building on Carter’s demythologising, our study develops a text-to-image AI visualisation of female figures in The Passion of New Eve through systematic prompt design and refinement, iterative evaluation, parameter adjustment, image-lexicon construction, and manual editing. By adjusting generated images to approximate the uncanny and grotesque bodily forms described in the novel, the study examines the tension between the culturally, socially, and commercially coded representations of gender embedded in generative AI systems and Carter’s alternative imaginaries of fluid and metamorphic subjectivities. However, our inquiry does not end with the technical evaluation of image quality or stylistic coherence. We propose a feminist critical framework that integrates aesthetic assessment of images (fidelity, authenticity, and affectivity) with post-identitarian critique of the generating process. In doing so, this project suggests a reciprocal relationship between feminist literature and generative AI: literature provides the ethical and conceptual grounding for critical AI practices, while AI enables feminist criticism to evolve into new multimodal, affectively charged terrains that exceed the limits of textual representation.

articles.title: Algorithmic commonsense knowledge and everyday TikTok practices: An ethnomethodological inquiry
articles.authors: Chia-Rong Tsao
articles.abstract: This study employs ethnomethodology to examine how TikTok users sustain and reconstruct algorithmic “commonsense knowledge” in everyday practices. Unlike previous research on algorithm awareness, algorithmic imaginaries, or folk theories of algorithms, this study analyzes how users’ algorithmic commonsense knowledge operates as an ongoing practical accomplishment. Based on 26 in-depth interviews with Taiwanese university students, I demonstrate that algorithmic commonsense knowledge functions through background expectancies and practical reasoning in users’ interactions with TikTok’s algorithmic system. The findings reveal how algorithmic power relations become naturalized through heterogeneous assemblages of material interfaces, user practices, and mutual accountability between users and algorithmic systems.

articles.title: Internet memes as mediating mechanisms: Between private emotion and collective identity among military reservist spouses in wartime
articles.authors: Hila Lowenstein-Barkai, Elie Friedman
articles.abstract: This study examines how digital memes function as a communicative repertoire through which military spouses mediate between personal experiences and collective identity within an online community during wartime. Focusing on a closed Facebook support group for Israeli military spouses during the first year of the Israel-Gaza war, we employ a mixed-methods approach, analyzing a corpus of 343 memes alongside in-depth interviews with creators to explore how these artifacts transform private affect into collective resources. We identified three central mediating mechanisms: (1) transforming personal experience into collective template; (2) processing overwhelming emotion through reflective distance; and (3) marking community boundaries through shared critique. Together, these mechanisms construct an interstitial space where personal and collective identities meet and mutually constitute one another. Rather than simply translating private experience into public discourse, meme affordances create a third space where the intensely personal remains visible while being absorbed into collective understanding. They allow creators to simultaneously embody their emotional experience and observe it from a distance. This process enables the articulation of experiences that are otherwise socially constrained, making the intensely personal collectively observable and fostering communal validation without violating normative expectations.

articles.title: Generative AI Use and Two-Wave Change in Well-Being and Ill-Being: A Pre- and Post-generative AI Era Panel Study
articles.authors: Hyunhee Kang, Young Min Baek
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly spreads, concerns about its impact on users’ mental health have surged. However, previous studies have yielded contradicting results owing to theoretical and methodological limitations. To address these gaps, this study investigates how generative AI adoption, usage time, and multidimensional AI dependency are related to two-wave changes in subjective well-being (self-esteem and life satisfaction) and ill-being (loneliness, anxiety, and depression). A two-wave longitudinal panel survey of 1,022 South Korean adults was conducted, with data collected in October 2022 (the pre-generative AI era) and March 2026 (the post-generative AI era), providing a prediffusion baseline against which change can be indexed. A multilevel modeling approach was used to examine within-subject and between-subject differences simultaneously. The results revealed that simple AI adoption and daily usage time were largely unrelated to changes in users’ subjective well-being or ill-being. However, a problematic form of AI use—specifically, withdrawal-type dependency characterized by psychological distress or frustration when unable to use AI—was associated with less decline in loneliness, with a suggestive but less robust pattern for depression, over time. These findings indicate that the use of generative AI is neither inherently beneficial nor intrinsically harmful. Instead of focusing merely on adoption or usage time, future research and practice should further examine maladaptive withdrawal-type AI dependency as a potential marker of less favorable mental-health change.

articles.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations
articles.authors: Giuseppe Riva, Stefania La Rocca, Brenda K. Wiederhold, Andrea Gaggioli
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human–AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

articles.title: Knowing You Seeing Me: The Role of Visual Contact During Video-Conferencing for Emotion Recognition and Mimicry
articles.authors: Michal Olszanowski, Aleksandra Fortuńska, Natalia Frankowska
articles.abstract: This study investigated how asymmetrical visual access in video-conferencing—specifically sender and receiver camera status—affects emotion recognition and facial mimicry. Ninety-one participants viewed bimodal (facial-vocal) or vocal-only displays of four emotions (anger, disgust, sadness, and happiness) while their own camera was either on or off. Recognition accuracy, intensity ratings, and facial muscle activity electromyography (EMG) were recorded. Results revealed that bimodal displays significantly enhanced recognition accuracy and perceived intensity compared with vocal-only signals, except for sadness. Emotional mimicry was most pronounced for affiliative displays (happiness and sadness) and was significantly stronger in the bimodal condition. Exploratory analyses suggested that the awareness of being observed (self-camera on) intensified smile-like reactions and improved the recognition of sadness. These findings suggest that mutual visibility facilitates emotion recognition and affiliative mimicry. The self-camera may function as a cue for public self-awareness, possibly sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor’s emotional signals. This research highlights the importance of multimodal communication in sustaining interpersonal synchronization during remote interactions.

articles.title: Does Fear of Missing Out Precede Problematic Internet Use, or the Reverse? A Two-Wave Cross-Lagged Study of Taiwanese Adolescents
articles.authors: Chi-Jung Sui, Mingchuan Hsieh, Ming-Hsueh Tsai
articles.abstract: Fear of missing out (FOMO), online social comparison, and problematic Internet use (PIU) are consistently correlated in adolescents, and influential models treat FOMO as a motivational antecedent of problematic use. This temporal ordering, however, has rarely been tested against its reverse. We analyzed the first two annual waves of the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study ( N = 8,311; Grade 7 to Grade 8; 49 percent girls) and estimated a latent cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) of PIU symptoms, FOMO, and online social comparison, using the survey weights and jackknife replicate standard errors. PIU symptoms predicted later FOMO (standardized β = 0.12, p < 0.001), and FOMO predicted later PIU ( β = 0.06, p = 0.017). The difference between the two directions was not statistically significant (Δ β = 0.06, 95 percent confidence interval [−0.01, 0.12], p = 0.093), and this remained so across eight analytic specifications, in which the estimates varied depending on the measurement model. FOMO and social comparison also predicted each other in the primary model but not in the ordinal sensitivity analyses, whereas social comparison did not predict later PIU, and all cross-lagged associations were small. These prospective associations do not support treating FOMO only as an antecedent of problematic use, because problematic use also preceded FOMO. A two-wave design cannot separate within-person change from stable differences between adolescents, so the findings describe prospective associations and await replication across three or more waves.

articles.title: The narrative self in Portuguese literary journalism: Irene Lisboa and Susana Moreira Marques
articles.authors: Jorge da Cunha, Isabel Tallysha-Soares
articles.abstract: This study examines the representation of the narrative ‘I’ in portrayals of Lisbon in the work of two Portuguese writer-journalists whose literary output spans distinct historical periods: Irene Lisboa during the second quarter of the twentieth century, and Susana Moreira Marques from 2013 onwards. The study investigates how the first-person narrator's subjective gaze discursively constructs a Lisbon that is both lived and interpreted, and how the urban space shapes processes of humanising the other. It also considers the tensions that arise between authorial voice, identity and journalistic-literary representation. An interpretivist framework is adopted together with a qualitative, inductive approach informed by narrative studies. Methodologically, it combines qualitative content and narrative analysis to examine how discursive and narrative strategies produce meanings related to the narrator's urban experience and their relationship with the other. Findings indicate that both authors deploy aesthetic and narrative devices that articulate a humanistic perspective on the city's inhabitants. Salient features include the centrality of time and memory, fragmentation and genre hybridity, and an attentive rendering of everyday life. Their writing is also shaped by immersion and urban wandering, alongside a pronounced authorial presence-hallmarks of literary journalism. Simultaneously, subjectivity, emotion and empathy contribute to an ethical approach to representing the other. Overall, the works align with the principles of literary journalism, combining narrative technique with sustained attention to the human experience of urban life.

articles.title: A Matter of Accessibility: A Guidelines-Based Accessibility Evaluation of Award-Nominated Video Games
articles.authors: Nadia Di Leo
articles.abstract: This study evaluates the accessibility of five games nominated for the Innovation in Accessibility award at The Game Awards 2025 : Assassin's Creed Shadows , Atomfall , DOOM: The Dark Ages , EA Sports FC 26 , and South of Midnight . Using the Game Accessibility Guidelines as an evaluation instrument, two evaluators independently assessed each title through a hybrid audit that combined a review of accessibility documentation with hands-on play. Each of the 121 guidelines was scored for applicability, implementation, and documentation status. Implementation rates ranged from 74.5% to 84.2%, confirming that all five titles provide substantial accessibility provisions. Compliance fell from basic guidelines (95.1% met across the sample) to advanced ones (52.3%), and the largest group of unmet guidelines concerned blind players. Documentation rates remained low. These findings indicate that even among the industry's most celebrated titles, accessibility remains unevenly distributed across impairment types and guideline complexity levels.

articles.title: GenAI governance maturity and divergent use pathways at work: sanctioned assimilation depth and shadow use
articles.authors: Stanley Y. B. Huang
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how employee-perceived generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) governance maturity relates to approved enterprise use and unauthorized public-tool use in data-sensitive work. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave survey of 750 knowledge workers in Taiwan was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Additional checks examine same-occasion measurement, available controls, sector sensitivity and an alternative assimilation-to-shadow-use path. Findings regulatory pressure and internal guideline salience were positively associated with governance maturity. Governance maturity was positively related to safe-to-use climate and perceived data exposure risk. The former was associated with sanctioned assimilation depth and task performance; the latter was negatively associated with shadow GenAI Use, which was positively related to employee creativity. These associations suggest a tension between reliable sanctioned performance and risk-laden exploration. Originality/value Sanctioned assimilation depth and shadow GenAI use are distinct appropriation modes, not opposite ends of one use continuum. Integrating institutional and socio-technical perspectives explains how governance differentiates the conditions attached to approved and unapproved channels without assuming that consumer-led workplace technology use is new.

articles.title: Understanding user agency and structural conditions in information system implementation: a study in industrial maintenance
articles.authors: Heini Ikävalko, Miia Martinsuo, Elviira Saarelma
articles.abstract: Purpose Users within the same organization may enact the same digital information system differently, creating diverse requirements and challenges for implementation. It is essential to view information system implementation as a process shaped by individuals' capacity to act within organizational structures, that is, through their agency. This study explores the manifestation of user agency and its associated structural conditions in information system implementation. Design/methodology/approach We examined users' experiences of information system implementation in two industrial companies' maintenance operations, through an interpretive qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews. Findings The study identifies four types of agency, namely eligible, estranged, skilled and motivated, and shows ways in which structural conditions of work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in information system users' work both enable and hinder user's capacity to act during information system implementation. Practical implications The identified agency types can help managers in tailoring information system implementation support. Acknowledging work design, collaborative practices and situated resources enhances users' capacity to act with the new system. Originality/value This study contributes by introducing a typology of user agency in information system implementation: it provides a fine-grained lens to explain why users facing the same information system enact it differently and extends enactment-oriented information system research on human agency. Showing how agency is conditioned by work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in users' unique work conditions, it addresses agency as part of the social and structural dynamics of information system implementation.

articles.title: Governing attention, triggering fatigue: how social media intrusiveness and regulatory focus shape perceived overload
articles.authors: Ali TotonchyFardMotlagh, Youying Wang, Wei Wang, Hefu Liu
articles.abstract: Purpose This study uses the attentional sovereignty perspective to examine how social media intrusiveness (presenteeism, anonymity, and flexibility) relates to perceived information overload, perceived social overload, and social media fatigue, and how regulatory focus moderates feature-overload relationships. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 386 social media users in China are analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling and hierarchical regression. Findings Presenteeism is positively associated with both types of perceived overload, whereas anonymity and flexibility show negative associations. Perceived information overload and perceived social overload mediate relationships between intrusive features and fatigue. Promotion and prevention focus exert feature-specific moderating effects, some of which differ from the hypothesized directions. Practical implications Platforms can reduce fatigue by offering simple, reversible controls over notifications, availability, audience visibility, and interaction timing rather than assuming that all intrusive features are harmful. Originality/value This study advances the fatigue literature by integrating the attentional sovereignty lens, differentiating two overload mediators, and revealing the moderating mechanism of regulatory focus in users' responses to social media intrusiveness.

articles.title: Won’t somebody please think of practitioners? Understanding practitioner engagement with academic information systems research
articles.authors: Cathal Doyle, Qianyi Li, Kristijan Mirkovski, Paul Benjamin Lowry
articles.abstract: Purpose This paper examines why practitioner engagement with academic Information Systems (IS) research remains limited despite the long-standing rigour-relevance debate. It reframes the issue as a knowledge adoption and translation problem by explaining how practitioners recognise, access, and use academic research in work practice. Design/methodology/approach Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 315 IS practitioners, primarily from the UK and the US, with a small component from New Zealand. The research model was tested using partial least squares path modelling. Bootstrapped mediation analysis examined indirect effects, and multivariate analysis of variance with follow-up analyses of variance assessed differences. Findings Innovation autonomy positively affected perceived content relevance, but not perceived communication relevance, suggesting that practitioner discretion helps practitioners recognise substantive value but does not resolve communication barriers embedded in academic research artefacts. Perceived communication relevance increased access intention to informal sources. In contrast, perceived content relevance increased access intention to both formal and informal sources, indicating that strong substantive relevance generates complementary rather than substitutive access pathways. Access to both informal and formal sources increased research engagement behaviour. Practical implications IS researchers should tailor dissemination to practitioner profiles and use clearer translational formats. IS journals should strengthen their mechanisms for practitioner-facing publications beyond conventional statements of practical implications. Originality/value The paper offers a practitioner-centred, empirically tested process model showing that engagement depends on perceived value, communication, and access pathways, rather than on relevance alone. The staged structure is used as a theoretical framework, while the empirical findings are interpreted as cross-sectional associations.

articles.title: Actualizing the external enablement of generative artificial intelligence: evidence from software new ventures
articles.authors: Jiyoung Kim, Joaquin Cestino, Tim Luca Greiner, Simon Hund
articles.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have been argued to enable entrepreneurial endeavors. Employing the external enablement framework, we examine how, if at all, the venture-level benefits offered by GenAI tools – termed GenAI enablement – are actualized in new ventures. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative design with 10 entrepreneurs in the software industry and five AI-entrepreneurship experts, we capture instances where entrepreneurs succeed or fail to capitalize on GenAI enablement and analyze the mechanisms underlying these different pathways. Findings Our findings lead to a model that outlines the actualization pathways of GenAI enablement, emphasizing that the properties of enablement (i.e. opacity, agency-intensity and outcome-variability) – beyond the mere availability of GenAI enablement – are crucial in explaining whether and how enablement is actualized. Research limitations/implications Given the small sample and specific research context during the early diffusion of GenAI, our findings warrant further examination across industries, countries and stages of technological diffusion. Future research could test and extend our model by examining the roles of outcome-variability and insufficient enablement in determining whether and how GenAI enablement is actualized, as well as how its actualization relates to venture performance. Originality/value Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and empirical investigation into the enabling influence of GenAI in entrepreneurship and business research, and provides conceptual refinements to the external enablement framework.

articles.title: Association between internet non-use and mortality risk among older adults: the explanatory contribution of social integration
articles.authors: Patrícia Silva, Gina Voss, Alice Delerue Matos, Roberto Martinez-Pecino
articles.abstract: Purpose Digital exclusion has emerged as an important dimension of social exclusion among older adults and has been associated with adverse health outcomes. However, its association with all-cause mortality and the potential role of social integration remain unclear. This study examined whether recent internet non-use was associated with all-cause mortality and explored the potential contribution of social integration. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), including 47,989 community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older from 18 countries. Internet non-use was defined as no internet use during the previous seven days. Country-stratified Cox proportional hazards models examined the association between internet non-use and mortality, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, depressive symptoms, and physical health. Mediation analyses evaluated the potential contribution of social integration. Findings Internet non-use was independently associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, depressive symptoms, and physical health. This association remained after accounting for social integration, although it was partially attenuated. Social integration explained part of the observed association, suggesting that it may represent a potential explanatory pathway linking internet non-use and mortality. Research limitations/implications Recent internet non-use was independently associated with higher all-cause mortality among older adults. Social integration accounted for part of this association, although additional pathways are likely to contribute. These findings support the interpretation of internet non-use as a marker of broader digital exclusion and highlight the importance of promoting digital inclusion and social participation in healthy ageing. Practical implications Policymakers should prioritize digital inclusion as a public health strategy. Programs promoting digital literacy and improving internet accessibility for older adults are essential not only for social integration but also as potential interventions to mitigate mortality risks associated with the digital divide. Social implications Non-use of the internet represents a critical barrier to contemporary social well-being. Addressing digital inequalities is a matter of social justice; fostering inclusive technological environments can enhance the social fabric and support the overall health and survival of aging populations. Originality/value This study extends previous research by examining, in a large multicountry European cohort, not only the association between recent internet non-use and all-cause mortality but also the potential explanatory contribution of social integration. These findings support the interpretation of internet non-use as a marker of broader digital exclusion and highlight the importance of promoting digital inclusion and social participation in healthy ageing.

articles.title: A History of Childhood Maltreatment and Marital Functioning: A Dyadic Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: Osnat Zamir, Ohad Szepsenwol, Ruby Charak, Inga Schalinski, Dana Lassri, Jessica Borelli
articles.abstract: A history of childhood maltreatment (CM) is a critical risk factor for marital challenges, but dyadic patterns of CM and relationship dynamics remain underexplored. This study utilized dyadic latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify distinct couple profiles based on both partners’ CM severity and marital functioning, focusing on marital quality, positive communication, and perceived partner responsiveness. The study further examined whether these profiles differ in posttraumatic stress and depressive symptoms. A sample of 393 mixed-sex Israeli married couples completed standardized self-report measures. LPA revealed four profiles: Low-Risk High-Functioning (LRHF; 85%), Moderate-Risk Distressed Couples (MRDC; 9.2%), High-Risk Wives Low-Functioning (HRWLF; 3.5%), and High-Risk Men Resilient Couples (HRMRC; 2.3%). Women in the HRWLF and men in the MRDC profiles, both with higher-than-average CM severity and lower marital functioning, reported higher levels of psychological symptoms. Conversely, women in the HRMRC profile, despite elevated CM severity, showed marital functioning similar to women in the LRHF group and reported the lowest psychological distress. This study advances the understanding of risk and resilience of couples in the context of CM, emphasizing the interplay between each partner’s CM severity, marital dynamics, especially perceived partner responsiveness, and gender. The findings highlight the need for trauma-informed, gender-sensitive couple interventions that strengthen relational functioning to buffer the psychological impact of CM history.

articles.title: Artificial Discursive Intimacy: A Relational Formation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Companions
articles.authors: Liang Cao, Shuyi Pan, Bibo Lin, Jindong Leo-Liu, Angel M. Y. Lin
articles.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots has given rise to a novel form of human–AI intimacy, yet its fundamental nature remains undertheorized. Drawing on a dialogical perspective, this study conceptualizes human–AI chatbot relationships as “artificial discursive intimacy” (ADI), a distinct relational formation in which intimacy is constituted through discourse with a disembodied algorithmic interlocutor, moving beyond the paradigm of human-to-human mediated intimacy. Based on in-depth interviews with 29 AI companion users, we identify four key differences between ADI and human discursive intimacy, including a shift from absent to activated presence, from reciprocity to unilaterality, from uncertainty to predictability and precarious safety, and from alterity to multi-dimensional mirroring. To understand how users navigate the ontological gap between human and AI, we propose a quadrant framework mapping human and AI social capabilities. This reveals dual animation processes of anthropomorphic animation, in which users project human embodied qualities onto AI, and robotomorphic animation, in which users internalize AI's machine-generated discursive patterns as relational ideals. Our findings suggest that ADI is sustained by a recursive interplay of these processes, with implications for how intimacy, relational selves, and human connection are being fundamentally reshaped in the age of AI.

articles.title: Navigating Infertility Together: The Influence of Romantic Attachment on Couple Outcomes—A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
articles.authors: Camilla Tacchino, Rosetta Castellano, Guyonne Rogier, Teresa Cocchiaro, Alessandro Dal Lago, Rocco Rago, Patrizia Velotti
articles.abstract: Infertility is a significant public health concern, profoundly affecting both individuals and couples. This systematic review and meta‐analysis aims to explore whether romantic attachment serves as a protective or risk factor in how couples navigate infertility diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes, with a specific focus on relational correlates. A systematic search was conducted across six databases from January 1, 2011, to February 3, 2025. Seventeen studies met the inclusion criteria, examining the link between romantic attachment and couple‐related psychological outcomes. Five of these studies were included in a meta‐analysis assessing the associations between attachment anxiety and avoidance and dyadic adjustment. Findings highlight significant associations between insecure attachment dimensions (both anxiety and avoidance) and reduced relationship and sexual satisfaction among individuals facing infertility. Meta‐analytic results revealed moderate negative associations between attachment insecurities and dyadic adjustment. Additionally, cross‐partner effects were observed, indicating that one partner's attachment style can impact the other's infertility experience. This study underscores the pivotal role of romantic attachment in managing infertility‐related challenges, distinguishing the distinct impacts of attachment anxiety and avoidance, and offering valuable clinical insights for supporting couples undergoing fertility treatments.

articles.title: The Effect of Perceived Similarity and Accuracy in Ideal Partner Preferences on Relationship Satisfaction
articles.authors: Sophia G. North, Karen R. Dobkins
articles.abstract: How partners perceive one another may be important for relationship satisfaction, particularly when those perceptions concern ideal partner preferences. The present study tested whether perceived similarity (alignment between one's own ideals and one's perceptions of a partner's ideals) and accuracy (alignment between one's perceptions of a partner's ideals and a partner's reported ideals) are associated with relationship satisfaction. A sample of 136 mixed‐gender couples ( N = 272), dating for an average of 16 months, reported their own ideals, their perceptions of their partner's ideals, and their relationship satisfaction. Actor‐Partner Interdependence Models (APIMs) revealed that individuals' perceived similarity predicted their own, and their partner's, relationship satisfaction. By contrast, accuracy did not predict relationship satisfaction, although exploratory analyses showed that other aspects of accuracy (e.g., the degree to which one perceives themselves as accurate about their partner) were associated with greater satisfaction. Taken together, these findings suggest that subjective beliefs about similarity and accuracy might be more strongly linked to relationship satisfaction than objective correspondence.

articles.title: When I See You Smile: Links Among Experienced Affect, Expressed Emotional Components, and Target Readability in a Supportive Interaction
articles.authors: Alexandrija Zikic, Michele Morningstar, Erin P. Macdonald, Laurence Jette, Lauren J. Human, Jennifer A. Bartz, Melanie A. Dirks
articles.abstract: Navigating supportive interactions is an important task of friendship that involves exchanging affective information. However, experienced affect is not always readable, and emotional expressions are not all equally helpful in conveying experienced affect. We examined associations between target readability (i.e., emotional expressive accuracy, or the degree to which individuals accurately communicate their experienced affect to others), and experienced and expressed emotional components (i.e., facial expressions and affect words), when seeking support from a friend. Participants ( N = 137 dyads, M age = 19.61 years, SD age = 1.34 years) took turns discussing problems they were having. To measure experienced affect, participants reported their positive and negative affect during the interaction. Expressed emotional components were participants' facial movements (i.e., eyebrow movements and smiles) and use of positive and negative affect words. To measure readability, observers continuously rated participants' affect during the interaction; their ratings were correlated with similar self‐ratings made by participants, and those correlations were averaged. Participants were more readable when they reported experiencing greater negative affect. In terms of expressed emotional components, participants were more readable when they had more eyebrow raises, and fewer eyebrow furrows and smiles. Results elucidate factors that contribute to effective communication of experienced affect when seeking support from friends.

articles.title: Do People Believe a Significant Other Means Significant Savings? Lay Beliefs About the Financial Cost of Relationships
articles.authors: Johanna Peetz, Geoff MacDonald
articles.abstract: People in relationships tend to be in a better financial position than people who are single due to income pooling, joint purchase savings, and cheaper leisure habits. Across three studies (combined N = 1058 US Americans), we examine single people's beliefs about whether romantic relationships save money or cost money relative to singlehood. Across studies, participants (especially men) tended to endorse beliefs that relationships cost money. Lay beliefs regarding the financial cost of relationships were negatively linked to relationship readiness and intent to find a partner in the next 6 months (Studies 1–3), suggesting these financial beliefs dissuade singles from partnering. Notably, implicit theories about the cost of relationships could be shifted: When participants were induced to focus on financial advantages (Studies 2 and 3), participants' beliefs in the costliness of relationships were attenuated, and there was a small condition effect on higher relationship readiness and intent to partner across studies. In sum, implicit theories about the financial cost of relationships appear to play a role in decisions about staying single versus partnering.

articles.title: When Messages About Science Get Old, Does Humor Make Them New?
articles.authors: Scarlett Sijia Liu, Nathan Walter
articles.abstract: In high-choice media environments, repeated persuasive messages often produce message fatigue, marked by disengagement and resistance. This research examines whether humor can mitigate fatigue. Across two studies spanning distinct domains and cultures, findings reveal a conditional role for humor. Study 1 ( N = 268) shows that humor reduces fatigue only among low-trust individuals. Study 2 ( N = 406) demonstrates that effectiveness depends on message design: incongruity humor reduces fatigue more than aggressive humor, particularly when paired with suggestive (vs. imperative) language. Collectively, humor is not a universal remedy but a strategic tool whose impact depends on audience characteristics and message features.

articles.title: A Meaning-Oriented Pathway From Science Fiction to Science Interest: The Role of Entertainment Motivations and Experiences
articles.authors: Yao Yao, Fangzhou Zhou, Jian Raymond Rui
articles.abstract: Characterized by imaginative and futuristic themes of science and technology, science fiction (sci-fi) may foster science interest, yet theory-based empirical evidence remains scant. Drawing on entertainment theories, we conducted a cross-sectional survey (Study 1, N = 517) and a retrospective survey (Study 2, N = 300). Results showed sci-fi engagement bridged both hedonic and eudaimonic motivations to science interest, while only eudaimonic motivation was directly linked to it. Recalling sci-fi (vs. comedy) films elicited stronger eudaimonic appreciation, which predicted heightened intentions to seek science information. Findings suggest that sci-fi can facilitate interest development mainly through a meaning-oriented pathway.

articles.title: Prevalence or Threat? How Misinformation Interventions Shape Veracity Discernment and Trust in Scientists
articles.authors: Myojung Chung, S. Mo Jones-Jang, Betty S. Lai
articles.abstract: Science misinformation poses two distinct problems: promoting inaccurate scientific beliefs and undermining trust in scientists. Yet little research has examined the psychological mechanisms through which interventions may address both problems. An experiment ( N = 832) compared accuracy prompts and threat-focused and efficacy-focused forewarning, examining perceived misinformation prevalence and threat as mediators. Both forewarning messages increased perceived prevalence and threat, but only threat was associated with better veracity discernment and greater trust in scientists. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing how widespread misinformation seems from how harmful it feels when examining how interventions shape veracity discernment and trust in scientists.

articles.title: Disenchanting the Epistemic Authority and Inevitability of AI: An Analysis of Factcheckers’ Perspectives and Professional Guidelines
articles.authors: Regina Cazzamatta, Augusto Santos
articles.abstract: As a sociotechnical practice, fact-checking integrates artificial intelligence (AI) while resisting “enchanted determinism” to preserve professional agency and epistemic authority. This study examines how fact-checkers in Europe and Latin America perceive AI affordances within their professional practices and how organizations articulate and govern AI use. Methodologically, the study is based on 50 qualitative interviews with practitioners and a thematic analysis of 18 publicly available AI guidelines and institutional documents. The findings suggest a distinction between instrumental optimism and epistemic disenchantment . While fact-checkers embrace AI’s functional affordances to enhance efficiency in tasks such as monitoring and data processing, they resist delegating the authority to determine truth to autonomous systems. At the organizational level, human-in-the-loop requirements formalize this distinction and operate as a form of boundary work that defines the limits of automation. We also identify a shared rationale for AI use across countries, which may reflect some degree of institutional convergence. However, this consensus coexists with a persistent “AI divide” shaped by contextual forces. Overall, the study shows how fact-checkers act as sociotechnical agents who “strip the magic” from AI, reaffirming human judgment as the field’s core epistemic foundation.

articles.title: Contextualizing Platform Power: A Comparative Study of Newspaper–Portal Dependency in South Korea and Japan
articles.authors: Joo-Young Jung, Misook Lee, Mikko Villi, Akira Tanaka, Yong-Chan Kim, Kaori Hayashi, Nando Malmelin
articles.abstract: This article examines how dominant news portals, Naver in South Korea and Yahoo Japan, shape power and dependency relations with mainstream newspapers under different national resource environments. Drawing on media system dependency theory, structuration theory, and normalization process theory, the study analyzes how senior newsroom leaders understand portal dependency, respond to portal control over key resources, and reflexively monitor the organizational consequences of those responses. Based on fifteen in-depth interviews with senior editors and executives across ten major news organizations, the analysis reveals variation within a shared pattern of portal centrality. In both countries, portals control important resources for audience access, visibility, and monetization, and newspapers continue many portal-related practices despite recognizing their costs. However, dependency differs in degree and form. In South Korea, limited alternatives make continued accommodation to Naver organizationally reasonable, while repeated portal-oriented practices further weaken direct audience relationships and intensify asymmetric dependency. In Japan, newspapers retain more diversified resources, including subscription revenues, distribution networks, advertiser relationships, and institutional access, enabling greater negotiation and partial reconfiguration of relations with Yahoo without eliminating dependency. The findings show that portal dependency is reproduced through the interaction of unequal resource configurations, reflexive monitoring, and repeated organizational practices. The study thus offers a context-sensitive and recursive account of platform power by showing how critical awareness of dependency may coexist with practices that sustain it, and how the availability of alternative resources shapes organizations’ capacity to modify those relations.

articles.title: The Hype Versus the Reality of Generative AI in Elections: The Case of the 2024 Indian Elections
articles.authors: Simon Chauchard, Kiran Garimella
articles.abstract: The 2024 Indian General Election was defined by pervasive warnings that generative AI would unleash a tsunami of deepfakes and fundamentally destabilize democratic processes. To empirically test these predictions, we analyzed over 5.5 million messages from more than 6,000 WhatsApp groups, obtained through a large-scale data donation project in India. Our findings reveal a profound disconnect between pre-election hype and ground truth: generative AI constituted only about 1.1 percent of the image dataset once corrected for the measured recall of our detection pipeline, a figure we treat as a lower bound, with no evidence of a viral “deepfake” epidemic. Furthermore, a qualitative taxonomy of this content reveals that the technology was rarely deployed for deception. Instead, it was primarily utilized for “phatic” labor—automating the production of hyper-stylized “Good Morning” greetings, religious iconography, and patriotic art. We argue that AI adoption was constrained by technological friction and by economic incentives, as traditional “cheapfakes” remained comparatively more cost-effective alternatives for political actors. These results challenge the prevailing focus on the threat of AI-driven messaging, suggesting that the technology may not always lead to epistemic disruption, but rather to the efficient reproduction of existing social rituals.

articles.title: When Elections End, Does Incivility? Examining Online Incivility Perceptions Across Four National Elections
articles.authors: Eliza Mitova, Laia Castro, Pamina Syed Ali, Michael Amsler, Yuan Zhang, Frank Esser
articles.abstract: Political incivility violates democratic, deliberative, and politeness norms, with repercussions for societal health. These repercussions are amplified in today’s digital environment, where social media platforms facilitate the expression and spread of incivility at an unprecedented global scale. Because incivility is subjective and context-dependent, its perception can only be fully understood through a joint consideration of individual factors and contextual conditions. To this end, we advance a three-level framework for examining incivility perceptions which conceptually maps the interdependence between micro-level individual factors and macro-national and meso-electoral specifics. We examine how well this framework plays out for perceptions of political incivility on social media across four nations with different media and political systems (Brazil, Spain, Switzerland, and the United States), drawing on a two-wave panel survey in the weeks leading up to and following their national elections (2022–2024). Contrary to our expectations, perceptions were highest in Brazil and the United States, the latter being the context whose permissive opportunity structures we expected to be most desensitizing. Change over the electoral period followed three distinct pathways: perceptions increased in Brazil, remained stable in Spain, and decreased in the United States and Switzerland, a pattern consistent with how decisively each electoral contest was resolved. Individual dispositions showed no uniform effects. Instead, their influence varied with national contexts. The findings suggest that online incivility perceptions may be primarily shaped by macro- and meso-level conditions, specifically the national political context and its electoral landscape. We conclude by discussing what the results imply for democratic resilience in increasingly uncivil information environments.

articles.title: Visual language games: A theoretical framework toward stylisation, defamiliarisation and interpretability in visual communication
articles.authors: Hadi Rahmati, Jessica Barness
articles.abstract: This article examines the relationships among stylisation, defamiliarisation and interpretability in visual communication. Drawing on Peirce’s semiotic theory, Barthes’s rhetoric of the image, Shklovsky’s concept of defamiliarisation and Arnheim’s Gestalt analysis, this study investigates how formal organisation and stylistic variation shape visual meaning. Rather than treating stylisation as a secondary aesthetic layer, the article positions it as a mechanism that modulates interpretive engagement. Interpretability is defined as the degree and range of semiotic and aesthetic engagement a visual work can sustain. Building on developments in visual semiotics, the framework distinguishes between figurative and plastic dimensions and examines how stylisation operates through their interaction. It further differentiates between plastic elements and plastic operations, showing how transformations, such as deformation, reorganise perceptual expectations and recalibrate interpretation. Drawing on Wittgenstein’s concept of language games, our framework understands visual communication as operating through what we call visual language games, in which conventions structure meaning, and expressive modulation shapes how those conventions are perceived. Stylisation, together with mediatic conditions and culturally situated visual literacy, recalibrates interpretive effort by configuring visual language in relation to visual familiarity, thereby guiding, disrupting or expanding meaning-making. The article proposes a visual interpretability spectrum in which stylisation configures visual language whose interpretation is mediated by visual familiarity, resulting in varying degrees of interpretive openness. By extending semiotic, formalist and perceptual perspectives, the framework clarifies how stylisation functions as a mechanism of defamiliarisation and interpretive calibration in visual communication, with implications for design practice, education and visual analysis.

articles.title: Framing authority and citizenship: Visual representations in Southeast Asia’s strategic public campaigns
articles.authors: Abhirama Swastyayana Dian Perdana, Mohammad Shihab
articles.abstract: This study examines how Southeast Asian governments construct symbolic authority and civic identity through visual state campaigns, focusing on Indonesia’s #SemuaWajibPakaiMasker and Singapore’s #TestTraceVaccinate – Together, Towards a New Normal . Although developed during the COVID-19 pandemic, these campaigns are analysed as artefacts of visual governance – texts that perform state legitimacy, model participation, and express ideological notions of citizenship. Using Kress and Van Leeuwen’s visual grammar and Machin and Mayr’s representational strategies, the study conducts a qualitative multimodal analysis of state-produced campaign videos by combining systematic visual coding with critical multimodal discourse analysis. The findings reveal contrasting visual logics: Indonesia’s campaign concentrates symbolic power in a singular leader, reflecting a paternalistic model of state – citizen relations, while Singapore’s campaign highlights diverse civic actors, suggesting a participatory model rooted in procedural legitimacy. These differences reflect not only political cultures but also institutional media histories and digital-era responses. By proposing a preliminary typology of visual governance styles in Southeast Asia, this study contributes to broader debates in visual communication, public relations, and strategic state messaging. It argues that public campaigns are not merely public health information tools, but performative spaces where the state imagines and enacts its relationship with the citizen. In this context, the image becomes a site of political work – where authority is not just shown, but shaped.
